'''Tayo''', also known as '''Saint-Louis Patois''' ({{langx|fr|patois de Saint-Louis}}), is a [[French-based creole languages|French-based Creole]] spoken on the outskirts of [[Nouméa]], the capital city of [[New Caledonia]]. It is spoken by about 3,000 people in the village of [[Saint-Louis, New Caledonia|Saint-Louis]], about {{cvt|15|km}} from Nouméa.<ref name=speedy2013>{{Cite journal|last=Speedy|first=Karin|date=2013|title=Mission Educated Girls in the 19th Century|journal=Shima: The International Journal of Research into Island Cultures|volume=7|issue=1|pages=60–79}}</ref>{{rp|63}} The language developed out of the contact of speakers of many different [[New Caledonian languages|Kanak languages]] in the mission, and the use of [[French language|French]] for official purposes and as the language of prestige.<ref name=speedy2013/>{{rp|61}} The language contains structural elements primarily from [[Melanesian languages]] and lexical elements mainly from French.<ref name=speedy2013/>{{rp|62}}

== History ==
[[File:SaintLouisEglise1.jpg|thumb|A church in Saint-Louis, New Caledonia]]
[[Saint-Louis, New Caledonia|Saint-Louis]] was founded as a [[Marist Brothers|Marist]] mission in 1860 in the early [[French colonial empire|French colonial period]] of the island, in order to convert the native [[Kanak people|Kanak]] population to [[Christianity]] and a European way of life.<ref name=speedy2013/>{{rp|63}} The missionaries took converts from surrounding Kanak tribes, especially the [[Cèmuhî language|Cèmuhi]], [[Drubea]] and [[Xârâcùù|Xârâcuu]] to live in the mission.<ref name=speedy2013/>{{rp|64}} Saint-Louis therefore became a highly [[Multilingualism|multilingual society]] with a diverse range of [[Kanak languages]] as well as French.<ref name=speedy2013/>{{rp|70}} In order for different ethnic groups to communicate and also because French was the language imposed by the missionaries, a simplified French became the language of communication and the native language of the next generation, which developed into Tayo Creole, mixing French vocabulary with mainly [[Melanesian languages|Melanesian language]] structures.<ref name=speedy2013/>{{rp|66}}

=== The Role of the Girls' Mission School ===
The girls school in [[Saint-Louis, New Caledonia|Saint-Louis]] has been widely considered instrumental in creating the conditions for the formation of Tayo, especially by Speedy (2013). There, Kanak girls were schooled in [[standard French]], and [[Kanak languages]] were forbidden, although in practice girls used many linguistic resources to communicate such as [[code-switching]], [[translation]] and the use of [[interlanguage]]s.<ref name=speedy2013/>{{rp|72}} These communicative practices resulted in a form of French with Melanesian structures.<ref name=speedy2013/>{{rp|72}} Men and boys meanwhile had less exposure to French working in the field. When the girls married husbands from the community their language had greater prestige than [[New Caledonian languages|Kanak languages]], thanks to the ideology of the missionaries.<ref name=speedy2013/>{{rp|70}} Therefore, despite the [[Multilingualism|societal multilingualism]] that had been the norm in New Caledonia at the time, in which children would learn the different native languages of their mother and father, couples communicated with each other and their children primarily in simplified French and this became the first language of the next generation, as Tayo Creole.<ref name=speedy2013/>{{rp|70}}

=== The impact of Reunion Creole ===
There has been a debate among linguists as to the impact of [[Réunion Creole|Reunion Creole]] in the formation of Tayo. Chaudenson proposed that Tayo was actually a ‘second generation’ creole, directly descended from the creole language of Reunionese migrants.<ref name=speedy2007>{{Cite journal|last=Speedy|first=Karin|date=2007|title=Reunion Creole in New Caledonia: What Influence on Tayo?|journal=Journal of Pidgin and Creole Languages|volume=22|issue=2|pages=193–230|doi=10.1075/jpcl.22.2.02spe}}</ref>{{rp|2}} He based this claim on phonological, lexical and grammatical similarities between the languages and the fact that some Reunionese had settled near Saint-Louis.<ref name=speedy2007/>{{rp|2}} Ehrhart and Corne refuted this claim, arguing that Tayo contains mainly Kanak structures.<ref name=speedy2007/>{{rp|3}} Speedy agrees that Tayo is largely structurally Melanesian, although she also argues that Reunion Creole was a type of French that interacted in the formation of Tayo.<ref name=speedy2007/>{{rp|32}}

== Grammar ==

=== Nouns ===
Tayo nouns do not display much internal [[Morphology (linguistics)|morphology]], with some number and [[definiteness]] information encoded in [[Grammatical modifier|modifiers]] and [[clitic]]s outside of the noun.<ref name=ehrhart2013>{{Cite journal|last1=Ehrhart|first1=Sabine|last2=Revis|first2=Melanie|date=2013|title=Tayo|url=https://apics-online.info/surveys/57|journal=The Survey of Pidgin and Creole Languages. Volume 2: Portuguese-based, Spanish-based, and French-based Languages.|publisher=Oxford University Press}}</ref>

==== Pluralisation ====
Tayo nouns can be [[plural]]ised with the modifier {{lang|cks|tule}}, which can be contracted to {{lang|cks|tle}} or {{lang|cks|te}}.<ref name=ehrhart2013>{{Cite journal|last1=Ehrhart|first1=Sabine|last2=Revis|first2=Melanie|date=2013|title=Tayo|url=https://apics-online.info/surveys/57|journal=The Survey of Pidgin and Creole Languages. Volume 2: Portuguese-based, Spanish-based, and French-based Languages.|publisher=Oxford University Press}}</ref> This is placed before the noun as shown in example (a):

(a)  {{lang|cks|tule	laser-la		le	travaj}}

PL	nun-the/this		SI	work

“The/these nuns work” <ref name=ehrhart2013>{{Cite journal|last1=Ehrhart|first1=Sabine|last2=Revis|first2=Melanie|date=2013|title=Tayo|url=https://apics-online.info/surveys/57|journal=The Survey of Pidgin and Creole Languages. Volume 2: Portuguese-based, Spanish-based, and French-based Languages.|publisher=Oxford University Press}}</ref>

==== Determiner/Demonstrative ====
Another nominal modifier is the [[clitic]] ''-la'' which can optionally follow nouns to introduce something new or to point to something within reach. This modifier, also present in [[New Caledonian French]], occurs frequently, especially with [[Anglicism|English loanwords]] and monosyllabic words.<ref name=ehrhart2013>{{Cite journal|last1=Ehrhart|first1=Sabine|last2=Revis|first2=Melanie|date=2013|title=Tayo|url=https://apics-online.info/surveys/57|journal=The Survey of Pidgin and Creole Languages. Volume 2: Portuguese-based, Spanish-based, and French-based Languages.|publisher=Oxford University Press}}</ref> This is demonstrated in example (b):

(b)	''ma	uver	kapoa-la''

I	open	tin-the/this

“I open the/this tin” <ref name=ehrhart2013>{{Cite journal|last1=Ehrhart|first1=Sabine|last2=Revis|first2=Melanie|date=2013|title=Tayo|url=https://apics-online.info/surveys/57|journal=The Survey of Pidgin and Creole Languages. Volume 2: Portuguese-based, Spanish-based, and French-based Languages.|publisher=Oxford University Press}}</ref>

==== Possession ====
[[Possession (linguistics)|Possession]] is denoted with the preposition ''pu'', placed after the possessed and before the possessor.<ref name=ehrhart2013>{{Cite journal|last1=Ehrhart|first1=Sabine|last2=Revis|first2=Melanie|date=2013|title=Tayo|url=https://apics-online.info/surveys/57|journal=The Survey of Pidgin and Creole Languages. Volume 2: Portuguese-based, Spanish-based, and French-based Languages.|publisher=Oxford University Press}}</ref> This is shown in example (c):

(c)	''fij		pu	ʃef''

daughter	PREP	chief

“The chief’s daughter” <ref name=ehrhart2013>{{Cite journal|last1=Ehrhart|first1=Sabine|last2=Revis|first2=Melanie|date=2013|title=Tayo|url=https://apics-online.info/surveys/57|journal=The Survey of Pidgin and Creole Languages. Volume 2: Portuguese-based, Spanish-based, and French-based Languages.|publisher=Oxford University Press}}</ref>

[[Personal pronoun]]s are divided into two categories, characterised by Ehrhart and Revis (2013) as dependent pronouns and independent pronouns. The dependent pronouns denote the [[Subject (grammar)|subject]] of a clause, and the independent pronouns denote a range of functions including the [[Object (grammar)|object]], emphatic subject, [[Reflexive pronoun|reflexive]] subject or [[Possession (linguistics)|possessor]].<ref name=ehrhart2013>{{Cite journal|last1=Ehrhart|first1=Sabine|last2=Revis|first2=Melanie|date=2013|title=Tayo|url=https://apics-online.info/surveys/57|journal=The Survey of Pidgin and Creole Languages. Volume 2: Portuguese-based, Spanish-based, and French-based Languages.|publisher=Oxford University Press}}</ref> In the dual and 1st and 2nd person plural, both types of pronoun have the same form.<ref name=ehrhart2013>{{Cite journal|last1=Ehrhart|first1=Sabine|last2=Revis|first2=Melanie|date=2013|title=Tayo|url=https://apics-online.info/surveys/57|journal=The Survey of Pidgin and Creole Languages. Volume 2: Portuguese-based, Spanish-based, and French-based Languages.|publisher=Oxford University Press}}</ref> Example (d) below shows the dependent pronoun sa in subject position and the independent pronoun ''mwa'' as a direct object. Meanwhile, example (e) shows the independent pronoun ''lja'' as an indirect object, as it is after the preposition ave.

(d)	''sa 	wa 	mwa''

they	see	me

“They see me”<ref name=ehrhart2013>{{Cite journal|last1=Ehrhart|first1=Sabine|last2=Revis|first2=Melanie|date=2013|title=Tayo|url=https://apics-online.info/surveys/57|journal=The Survey of Pidgin and Creole Languages. Volume 2: Portuguese-based, Spanish-based, and French-based Languages.|publisher=Oxford University Press}}</ref>

(e)	''nu	tro	aːᵐbete	ave	lja		depi	taler''

we	too	annoyed	with	him/her	since	just.now

“We too are annoyed with him since just now”<ref name=ehrhart2013>{{Cite journal|last1=Ehrhart|first1=Sabine|last2=Revis|first2=Melanie|date=2013|title=Tayo|url=https://apics-online.info/surveys/57|journal=The Survey of Pidgin and Creole Languages. Volume 2: Portuguese-based, Spanish-based, and French-based Languages.|publisher=Oxford University Press}}</ref>

Independent pronouns can also function as emphatic subjects. In these cases, the dependent pronoun functions like a clitic, characterised by Ehrart and Revis (2013) as a subject index.<ref name=ehrhart2013>{{Cite journal|last1=Ehrhart|first1=Sabine|last2=Revis|first2=Melanie|date=2013|title=Tayo|url=https://apics-online.info/surveys/57|journal=The Survey of Pidgin and Creole Languages. Volume 2: Portuguese-based, Spanish-based, and French-based Languages.|publisher=Oxford University Press}}</ref> This is shown in example (f):

(f)	''mwa	ma 	malad''

I	I (SI)	sick

“I (emphatic) am sick”<ref name=ehrhart2013>{{Cite journal|last1=Ehrhart|first1=Sabine|last2=Revis|first2=Melanie|date=2013|title=Tayo|url=https://apics-online.info/surveys/57|journal=The Survey of Pidgin and Creole Languages. Volume 2: Portuguese-based, Spanish-based, and French-based Languages.|publisher=Oxford University Press}}</ref>

A final use for independent pronouns is in [[possessive]] constructions. These are identical to how possession is expressed with nouns, with the independent pronoun placed after the possessive preposition pu,<ref name=ehrhart2013>{{Cite journal|last1=Ehrhart|first1=Sabine|last2=Revis|first2=Melanie|date=2013|title=Tayo|url=https://apics-online.info/surveys/57|journal=The Survey of Pidgin and Creole Languages. Volume 2: Portuguese-based, Spanish-based, and French-based Languages.|publisher=Oxford University Press}}</ref> as shown in example (g):

(g)	''kas	pu	mwa''

house	PREP	me

“My house” (Ehrhart & Revis 2013){{Reflist|group=Note|refs=
<ref name=Note04>Ehrhart and Revis describe ''le'' as a 3rd person marker for both 3rd person singular and plural based on their analysis of data from the 1980s and 1990s. However, they admit that modern Tayo uses ''le'' for all persons, often announcing a subject to come.</ref>
</ref>
<ref name=Note05>While speakers recognise ''lie'' as the more correct form for the 3rd person singular independent pronoun, their most common pronunciation is ''lje''.</ref>
</ref>
}}

==== Imperatives ====
[[Imperative mood|Imperative]] verbs are formed with an unmodified verb base,<ref name=ehrhart2013>{{Cite journal|last1=Ehrhart|first1=Sabine|last2=Revis|first2=Melanie|date=2013|title=Tayo|url=https://apics-online.info/surveys/57|journal=The Survey of Pidgin and Creole Languages. Volume 2: Portuguese-based, Spanish-based, and French-based Languages.|publisher=Oxford University Press}}</ref> as in example (i):

(i)	''<sup>n</sup>desa		<sup>n</sup>de	lao,	twa''

come.down	from	up	you

“Come down from up there, you!”<ref name=ehrhart2013>{{Cite journal|last1=Ehrhart|first1=Sabine|last2=Revis|first2=Melanie|date=2013|title=Tayo|url=https://apics-online.info/surveys/57|journal=The Survey of Pidgin and Creole Languages. Volume 2: Portuguese-based, Spanish-based, and French-based Languages.|publisher=Oxford University Press}}</ref>

==== Causatives ====
The marker ''fe'' is said before a verb to denote a [[causative]] action,<ref name=ehrhart2013>{{Cite journal|last1=Ehrhart|first1=Sabine|last2=Revis|first2=Melanie|date=2013|title=Tayo|url=https://apics-online.info/surveys/57|journal=The Survey of Pidgin and Creole Languages. Volume 2: Portuguese-based, Spanish-based, and French-based Languages.|publisher=Oxford University Press}}</ref> as in example (j):

(j)	''la	fe	plan	ver-la''

s/he	make	full	glass-the/this

“He filled the glass”<ref name=ehrhart2013>{{Cite journal|last1=Ehrhart|first1=Sabine|last2=Revis|first2=Melanie|date=2013|title=Tayo|url=https://apics-online.info/surveys/57|journal=The Survey of Pidgin and Creole Languages. Volume 2: Portuguese-based, Spanish-based, and French-based Languages.|publisher=Oxford University Press}}</ref>

=== Questions ===
[[Yes–no question|Polar questions]] are formed the same way like a statement, but with [[High rising terminal|rising intonation]], like is often done in spoken French.<ref name=ehrhart2013>{{Cite journal|last1=Ehrhart|first1=Sabine|last2=Revis|first2=Melanie|date=2013|title=Tayo|url=https://apics-online.info/surveys/57|journal=The Survey of Pidgin and Creole Languages. Volume 2: Portuguese-based, Spanish-based, and French-based Languages.|publisher=Oxford University Press}}</ref> This is shown in example (k):

(k)	''ta	kone	ke	se	mama		pu	lja?''

you	know	that	PRESV	mother	POSS	him/her

“Do you know that she is his/her mother?”<ref name=ehrhart2013>{{Cite journal|last1=Ehrhart|first1=Sabine|last2=Revis|first2=Melanie|date=2013|title=Tayo|url=https://apics-online.info/surveys/57|journal=The Survey of Pidgin and Creole Languages. Volume 2: Portuguese-based, Spanish-based, and French-based Languages.|publisher=Oxford University Press}}</ref>

Content questions likewise are phrased like statements, except with an [[Interrogative word|interrogative pronoun]] in place of a [[noun phrase]],<ref name=ehrhart2013>{{Cite journal|last1=Ehrhart|first1=Sabine|last2=Revis|first2=Melanie|date=2013|title=Tayo|url=https://apics-online.info/surveys/57|journal=The Survey of Pidgin and Creole Languages. Volume 2: Portuguese-based, Spanish-based, and French-based Languages.|publisher=Oxford University Press}}</ref> shown in example (l):

(l)	''ta	war	ki?''

you	see	who

“Who did you see?”<ref name=ehrhart2013>{{Cite journal|last1=Ehrhart|first1=Sabine|last2=Revis|first2=Melanie|date=2013|title=Tayo|url=https://apics-online.info/surveys/57|journal=The Survey of Pidgin and Creole Languages. Volume 2: Portuguese-based, Spanish-based, and French-based Languages.|publisher=Oxford University Press}}</ref>

==== Structural Formation ====
Siegel's (2008) analysis of [[Tense–aspect–mood|tense, mood and aspect]] marking in Kanak [[Stratum (linguistics)|substrate]] languages and Tayo Creole supports the theory that structural features from substrate languages (i.e. in this case, the [[New Caledonian languages|Kanak languages]]) are mostly likely to transfer into the [[Creole language|creole]] when they are shared by most of the substrate languages, and the [[lexifier]] language (i.e. in this case, [[French language|French]]).<ref name=siegel2008>{{Cite book|last=Siegel|first=Jeff|title=The emergence of Pidgin and Creole languages|publisher=Oxford University Press|year=2008|location=New York}}</ref>{{rp|214}} For example, [[future tense]] was marked in two out of three languages analysed as a pre-verbal tense marker. French also frequently express future tense using the verb ''aller'' (‘go’), as a pre-verbal marker. As this verb is most often realised in the 3rd person singular form ''va'', this form was transferred into Tayo Creole as the future tense marker.<ref name=siegel2008>{{Cite book|last=Siegel|first=Jeff|title=The emergence of Pidgin and Creole languages|publisher=Oxford University Press|year=2008|location=New York}}</ref>{{rp|216}} Likewise, [[Continuous and progressive aspects|progressive aspect]] marking occurs in all three languages, and French uses the phrase ''en train de'' with a similar function in pre-verbal position. As such, ''atra <sup>n</sup>de'' was transferred into the creole language as a pre-verbal progressive marker.<ref name=siegel2008>{{Cite book|last=Siegel|first=Jeff|title=The emergence of Pidgin and Creole languages|publisher=Oxford University Press|year=2008|location=New York}}</ref>{{rp|215}}

== Sociolinguistic situation ==
Tayo is in a [[Diglossia|diglossic]] relationship with French, with French having higher prestige and used in institutions such as education and in jobs, and Tayo mainly relegated to private homes.<ref name=parish2017>{{Cite journal|last1=Bissoonauth|first1=Anu|last2=Parish|first2=Nina|date=2017|title=French, English or Kanak Languages? Can Traditional Languages be Sustained in New Caledonia?|journal=Journal of Multidisciplinary International Studies|volume=14|issue=2|pages=39–53}}</ref>{{rp|43}} Tayo is often denigrated as ‘bad French’, with a Tayo speaking woman stating that as a child she was forbidden from speaking Tayo.<ref name=parish2017>{{Cite journal|last1=Bissoonauth|first1=Anu|last2=Parish|first2=Nina|date=2017|title=French, English or Kanak Languages? Can Traditional Languages be Sustained in New Caledonia?|journal=Journal of Multidisciplinary International Studies|volume=14|issue=2|pages=39–53}}</ref>{{rp|47}} A survey conducted by Bissonauth & Parish found that out of eight respondents who reported understanding Tayo, only three reported using it regularly.<ref name=parish2017>{{Cite journal|last1=Bissoonauth|first1=Anu|last2=Parish|first2=Nina|date=2017|title=French, English or Kanak Languages? Can Traditional Languages be Sustained in New Caledonia?|journal=Journal of Multidisciplinary International Studies|volume=14|issue=2|pages=39–53}}</ref>{{rp|47}}

In a 2015 study by the [[University of Technology Sydney]] (UTS), all three respondents (a male senator aged over 60, a female student aged under 20 and a female museum community liaison officer in her 40s) who reported speaking Tayo were also multilingual (with all three also speaking [[Drehu language|Drehu]] and [[New Caledonian French|French]], and the two women also speaking [[English language|English]]). The three respondents all lived on the outskirts of [[Greater Nouméa]], being from [[La Conception, New Caledonia|La Conception]], [[Saint-Louis, New Caledonia|Saint-Louis]] and [[Yaté]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://epress.lib.uts.edu.au/journals/index.php/portal/article/view/5378/6151|title=French, English or Kanak languages? Can Traditional Languages and Cultures be Sustained in New Caledonia?|first1=Anu|last1=Bissoonauth|first2=Nina|last2=Parish|publisher=[[UTS Library]]|date=31 January 2017}}</ref>
